narrative_structure: A regular five-act tragedy in blank verse with a single moral experiment as its skeleton; the delay, the counting of the days, and the return form the mechanical centre, and the scenes of the court supply the pressure that tests it.
principal_characters: Dionysius, tyrant of Syracuse; Damon, the hostage for his friend's life; Pythias, the condemned philosopher; the courtiers and officers of the tyrant
literary_form: Tragedy
meter_and_prosody: Correct and sustained blank verse in the declamatory school of the early nineteenth century, with set speeches of friendship and of tyranny and little lyrical experiment; the line is regular and the caesura frequent, fitted for declamation by the tragedy actors of the patent houses.
historical_context: Written after the author's removal from Kilkenny to London, where his drawings and his Irish tales made him known, and produced in the season when Covent Garden was reviving classical and moral tragedy for a mixed house. The play's subject had an English schoolroom currency through the eighteenth-century versions of the legend, and its treatment belongs to the Regency taste for proofs of virtue made in the presence of a tyrant.
literary_significance: Damon and Pythias was the most performed Irish tragedy of the 1820s and remained a stock piece of provincial and declamatory recitation for half a century, giving the legend of friendship a modern theatrical form. It is also the central document of the author's reputation and the point at which the question of joint Irish dramatist authorship has been argued.
attribution_notes: The play is constantly said to have been a joint work with an older Irish dramatist; the author's biographer denies the shared claim, and the first edition and the contemporary accounts carry the Kilkenny writer's name alone. The matter remains unresolved, and the record here follows the printed attribution.
bibliographical_notes: First performed at Covent Garden on 28 May 1821 and printed shortly after in London; the play went through several editions and was repeatedly reissued with the author's tales; the production was mounted by one of the two patent houses with its leading tragedy actor.

title: Revelations of the Dead-Alive
description: A tale of premature burial published in 1824, in which a man laid out and consigned to the grave returns to life unseen and learns what the living really think of him. The book is a domestic romance of a trading town, and its machinery of the coffin, the vault, and the resumption of identity makes it one of the earliest English prose treatments of the dead-alive subject. Its exposure of the greed that waits on a supposed death gives it a place in the lineage that runs from the Gothic tale to sensation fiction.
plot_or_argument: The hero, a man of substance in an Irish market town, is struck down and pronounced dead, and is laid in his coffin while the household settles into mourning that is mostly calculation. Restored to consciousness and to life within the place of burial, he escapes and keeps himself unknown, watching the conduct of those who had an interest in his death, and hearing their claims, hopes, and exposures. The later developments turn on the discovery of the living man, on the disappointment of the expecting heirs, and on the punishment or confoundment of those who had profited by the funeral. The tale's interest is the disclosure of character by the assurance that a man cannot hear it.
narrative_structure: A continuous third-person tale of single design, built on the secret survival of the hero and on the successive revelations his observation produces; it closes with the public unmasking that the plot has deferred.
principal_characters: the buried man who returns; the household and kinsfolk expecting his estate; the friends and creditors whose conduct the watch exposes; the town officers and undertakers of the funeral
literary_form: Gothic Novel and Romance of Terror
historical_context: Published between the author's tragedy and his Irish tales, in a decade much exercised by the fear of live burial, by the anatomy and the watch-house, and by the newspaper case of the coffin opened too late; the tale draws on a stock of popular terror already worked in periodical fiction and in the German tale. Its town setting belongs to the provincial Irish life the author was simultaneously putting into the O'Hara tales.
literary_significance: Revelations of the Dead-Alive is an early and influential English treatment of the premature-burial terror as a device for social exposure rather than for simple horror, and it anticipates the resurrection plots of later sensation and detective fiction. It also shows the range of an author otherwise classified by his national tales.
attribution_notes: Single authorship and undisputed; the volume carries the writer's name and no share has been claimed for his brother or collaborators.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London in 1824 in a small volume, subsequently reprinted within the collected tales and in modern facsimile; the text has been revised in later editions of the author's works.

title: The Tales of the O'Hara Family, First Series
alternative_titles: Tales of the O'Hara Family; by the Author of 'Damon and Pythias'. First Series
description: The first series of the national tales of a Kilkenny peasant family, published in 1825 and written in collaboration between two brothers, one of whom supplied the historical and topographical groundwork and both of whom share the narrative voice. The numbers give the cabin, the faction fight, the agrarian combination, and the phantom of the fetch in an Irish speech and at Irish length. The series founded the vogue of the Irish peasant tale and long stood as the standard account of the country people before the Famine.
plot_or_argument: The Fetches tells of the double or phantom seen before a death, of a murdered man whose fetch appears to his kin, and of the country rules by which such an appearance is read, making the supernatural a matter of evidence and of neighbourhood testimony. John Doe; or, The Peep o' Day gives the agrarian war of the secret combinations, the cottier's hatred of the middleman and of the tithe, the midnight burning and the broken contract, and the fate of a family caught in the faction. Crohoore of the Bill-hook follows a woman of the out-lawed countryside who leads the boys in the agrarian rising and is hunted to her end. The series is held together by the O'Hara household and its neighbours, whose talk and genealogy frame the tales.
narrative_structure: A framed series of independent tales told by and about one family, with a narratorial voice that reports Irish speech and supplies the historical and agrarian explanation inside the story; the series is not a continuous novel.
principal_characters: the O'Hara household and its dependants; the murdered man whose fetch is seen; the cottier families of the agrarian combination; Crohoore of the Bill-hook, the woman leader of the boys; the middlemen and the rural police
literary_form: The Sketch and Character Tale; Prose Fiction and the Early Novel
historical_context: Written in the years after the Act of Union and before the agitation for emancipation reached its crisis, out of the Kilkenny world of the hedge-school, the faction fight, and the agrarian association, and published at the moment when the national tale was the most prestigious form in British fiction. The brothers' earlier training as artists accounts for the series' emphasis on costume, cabin interior, and local scene, and one of them had been a pupil of the national drawing academy.
literary_significance: The first series of the O'Hara tales established the Irish peasant narrative as the dominant mode of the 1820s and supplied much of the vocabulary in which the fetch, the combination, and the cottier's grievance were discussed in English. Its collaborative authorship also makes it a standard instance of joint production in the national tale.
attribution_notes: Collaborative: the two brothers share the series, with one of them understood to have written the woman-led agrarian tale and to have supplied the historical and topographical matter; early reviews and later biographies divided the numbers unequally between them.
bibliographical_notes: First published in London and Dublin in 1825 in small volumes as the first series, with the attributing phrase 'by the author of Damon and Pythias'; a second series followed, and the whole was frequently reprinted and translated.
